newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka coalition's three-year rule a mixed bag.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka coalition's three-year rule a mixed bag.

text.p: Sri Lanka's ruling People's Alliance (PA), which won power three years ago promising to bring peace to the war-torn nation, can claim military victories against the rebels but a political solution to the crisis remains elusive.

The seven-party alliance has also failed to deliver on other election pledges like abolishing the executive presidency, but politicians and analysts said people were still optimistic if only because of the leadership charismatic President Chandrika Kumaratunga had provided.
"Chandrika is a lot more popular than the government. She is holding everything together," said Pakiasothy Saravanamuttu, a political analyst.
"Most people don't blame the government for the continuation of the war. There is no bitter sense of let down, no hostility towards the government," said Jehan Perera, a political columnist.

Kumaratunga's popularity was evident in the PA's thumping victory in local government elections in March, where the government, which completes three years in power on August 16, won 193 of the 238 councils that were contested.
The coalition win in 1994, which ended the 17-year-rule of United National Party (UNP), had raised expectations among minority Tamils of a quick resolution of the ethnic war.

The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the fighting, now in its 15th year. The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, the rebels seeking a homeland in the north and east, say the toll is higher.
Peace talks with the LTTE collapsed in early 1995 after the guerrillas sank two naval boats in the eastern port city of Trincomalee.
The military has not lessened its pressure on the separatists since, even while losing hundreds of men in rebel attacks.

Government troops drove the LTTE out of their long-time stronghold of Jaffna peninsula last year, and have since launched a campaign to open a vital highway through rebel territory to the peninsula where half a million Tamils live.
Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar told Reuters recently that the government was seeking a politico-military solution to the crisis as there was no other way to end it.

But while the government's military campaigns have made some headway in the past three years, its efforts to find a political solution to the ethnic crisis have become stuck in parliament debate due to a lack of consensus among political parties.
"There is disappointment among the Tamils that a political settlement has not materialised," said Murugasu Sivasithamparam, leader of the moderate Tamil United Liberation Front (TULF).
"The devolution proposals that she (Kumaratunga) put forward last August were progressive, but since then progress has been very slow," Sivasithamparam told Reuters.

The government is proposing a new constitution as part of a peace package that includes devolution of powers to administrative units in a bid to partly meet the LTTE's demand for a separate homeland for Tamils.
Gamini Peiris, minister of justice and constitutional affairs and the chief architect of the peace package, believes considerable progress has been made on this front.
"It is a matter which will touch dearly the lives of the people. It is slowly taking shape," he said.

Kumaratunga is scheduled to launch a nationwide campaign in late August to explain the proposals to the people, which analysts say is an effort to drum up their support and push the opposition United National Party (UNP) to support them in parliament.

In April this year, the PA and UNP agreed to take a "common approach" to resolve the protracted war, but the opposition has yet to pledge its support for the new constitution, saying it would wait for a final draft.
"The government has not taken steps to implement its election promises. Neither have they been able to bring peace to north and east," UNP leader Ranil Wickremesinghe told Reuters.
"We are worse off than we were three years ago."
If the devolution package or some other political solution is not found soon, the government will be forced to continue with the war, further hitting the country's economy.
"This could make people disillusioned with the government", Saravanamuttu said.
